name: test-data-builder
intent: Give each domain type used in tests a builder that starts from valid, commonly used defaults, so a test states only the data its assertion depends on and everything else is supplied correctly without being mentioned.
problem: Strict constructors and immutable value objects make test setup a chore: every test that needs an object must supply all constructor arguments, so tests fill up with values that have nothing to do with the behaviour under test, break whenever a constructor argument or the object's structure changes, and copy the same construction code from test to test. The ready-made fixtures of an object mother remove the repetition but not the variation - every slightly different case adds another factory method, and the mother degenerates into duplicated code or a swarm of methods holding a single new statement.
context: Applies to test suites over a domain model whose objects have many required fields or cross-field invariants, where each test varies only a small part of the data and a valid instance can be constructed without external systems. It is language-neutral but pays off most where the language lacks named/default arguments or copy-with-modification, and it belongs to the test sources: production code keeps its own constructors and must not depend on a builder whose defaults are chosen for tests.
benefits: Tests state only the data their assertion depends on: everything else comes from defaults, so a test reads as the behaviour under test rather than as object construction.
Valid defaults are defined once per type, so a new required constructor parameter or invariant is fixed in one place while the existing tests keep compiling.
Variation is cheap: stated as named overrides rather than one more factory method per case, which avoids the object mother's head-on collision with variability.
Names travel with the values: overriding by field name removes the silent positional-argument swap that raw constructor calls suffer from and makes the variation self-documenting.

Builders compose: a builder for a nested value becomes a default inside the enclosing builder, so whole graphs are assembled without repetition, and a but()/reuse helper derives similar objects from existing ones.
The team gains a shared vocabulary of static factories (aUser(), anInvoice()) that reads like the domain, so fixture data is easy to find and evolve.
tradeoffs: Boilerplate per type: every domain class gets a builder with duplicated default values that must be maintained against the constructor, a cost annotated processors and codecs only partly remove.
Defaults are a second specification of validity: they can drift from the domain's own constructor and validation, letting tests exercise objects that cannot occur in production (misleading validity).
Default overfit: an assertion that depends on a defaulted value the test never mentions silently changes meaning when that default is edited - the object mother's coupling fault in weaker form.
Test-only back doors (withId(), withInvalidState()) let tests construct impossible states the production path would reject, so the test proves nothing about that path.
Mutable builder instances are state traps: reusing one across tests leaks overrides and produces order-dependent failures, so builders must be treated as single-use accumulators.
Up-front cost is not repaid for small, stable objects: for a class with two fields that barely varies, the builder, its factory and its defaults are more code than the constructor call they replace.
The pattern forces placement and lifecycle decisions - test-only sources, generic versus concrete builders, product constructor visibility - that a plain helper or a copy-with expression does not.

participants.responsibility: Per-type construction helper that holds a safe value for every field, exposes named override methods, and produces the real domain object on build() (or via the language's copy-with/update idiom).
The commonly used, domain-valid values the builder starts from, so every field the test does not mention is already supplied correctly.
Named entry point (aUser(), anInvoice()) that returns a fresh builder and gives the test its domain vocabulary; also where a but()/similar-object helper hangs off.
States only the fields its assertion depends on, then asks the builder for the product; never assembles the graph by hand or edits the result afterwards.
The entity or value object being built; unaware of the builder and still constructed through its own real constructor and validation, so a built instance is legal by construction.

use_cases: Unit tests over domain types with many constructor parameters and cross-field invariants (invoices, users, policies) where each test cares about one or two values.
Mock-based interaction tests that must hand a valid collaborator object to the system under test with e.g. only its id varied to observe request routing.
Bug-reproduction tests: the builder encodes the standard valid case and the test states only the faulty value from the report.
Suites with many test classes over the same domain fixtures (payroll, insurance, orders) that need per-test variation rather than a handful of canned objects.
Table-driven or property-style tests over one dimension: build the valid base once and override that dimension for each case.
Integration tests that need a complete, plausible object graph (nested entities, collections, ids) deviating in a single field.

factory_bot (thoughtbot) for Ruby/Rails: one factory per class holding a minimal valid set of default attributes, with tests overriding only the fields under test at call time (build(:user, email: "bad@example.com")) - the builder shape generalized into a library.

factory_boy for Python: class-based factories declare the default keyword arguments for the target class' __init__ (Meta.model), and each test overrides just what it asserts (UserFactory.build(first_name="Joe")), with factory inheritance standing in for object-mother variants.

Instancio for Java implements the same contract generically: create(Person.class) populates every field, and .set(field(Person::getName), "Homer") overrides only the fields the test names - its user guide states the goal as populating everything you are not interested in.
avoid_when: The object has one or two fields and tests construct it inline: a constructor call states the data more directly than a builder adds indirection.
One or two fixed fixtures are needed everywhere and never vary: a plain factory function or constant (an object-mother-style helper) is simpler and leaves the variation machinery unused.
The data must be random or generated per run (property-based tests, load data): use a generator or faker with shrinking instead of canned defaults.
The language makes the override step native (copy(), with, spread, struct update): a hand-written builder class is often pure boilerplate - keep the default factory and use the native update.
The domain already offers named constructors for the only legal shapes (aggregate factories, smart constructors): duplicating them in a test builder adds a second, weaker specification.
The test needs an invalid object to check a rejection path: builders must not grow back doors, so hand the invalid input explicitly or use a test double.
anti_patterns: The builder without defaults: every field must still be set in every test, so the builder is a worse constructor with extra steps and the assertion stays buried in setup.
Back-door setters: withId, withInvalidState or forceX methods that bypass validation, letting tests construct states production rejects and hiding the behaviour the test claims to check.
Default overfit: assertions that depend on defaulted values nobody in the test mentions; editing a default silently rewrites the expected result and the test stops checking anything.
God builder / global TestData module: one builder for unrelated types with duplicated defaults, or a builder promoted as the production construction API because it was a convenient default factory.
Mutable builder reuse: keeping a half-populated builder in a field or singleton and amending it per test, producing order-dependent, unexplainable failures.
Builder as workflow: build() starts hitting the database, advancing clocks or filing events, turning a unit fixture into order-dependent integration setup.
design_principles: A test should state only what it asserts; everything else must be supplied by the design, not by the reader's attention.
Single source of truth for 'valid': defaults live in one place per type and run through the domain's real constructor and validation.
Don't repeat fixture construction across tests (DRY in test code) - but never buy reuse with coupling to canned values.
Immutability and value semantics first: the builder constructs a valid immutable object instead of having the test mutate one field at a time.
Intention-revealing interfaces: aUser().withEmail(...) names the domain concept and the varying value, unlike a positional constructor call.
best_practices: Give every field a valid, boring default and one static factory per type (aUser(), anInvoice()); keep defaults and builders in the test sources.
Build through the product's real constructor; never add test-only setters that bypass validation or invariants.
Treat builders as single-use: return a fresh builder from the factory in each test and make override methods' mutation/return semantics explicit.
Add but()/partial-builder helpers for creating similar objects and compose nested builders instead of flattening graphs.
Keep defaults clearly arbitrary and never assert on a value the test did not set - if a test cares about a field, override it explicitly.
Prefer the language's native update mechanism (copy, with, spread, struct update) where it exists; reserve hand-written builders for conditional or validated construction.

Keep builders honest against change: a mandatory build() or a struct update that fails to compile when the product changes is cheaper than a silent mismatch between defaults and constructor arguments.
sources: Pryce, N., Test Data Builders: an alternative to the Object Mother pattern (2007) - the pattern's origin, with its four builder rules (a field per constructor parameter, commonly used or safe defaults, a build method, chainable override methods).

Freeman, S. & Pryce, N., Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests, Addison-Wesley (2009) - Chapter 22, Constructing Complex Test Data (Test Data Builders, Creating Similar Objects, Combining Builders), pp. 257-264.
Bloch, J., Effective Java (3rd ed., 2018) - Item 2: Consider a builder when faced with many constructor parameters.
